transfer receiver and an incorrect no-skill knockout baseline.

Qwen3-8B at $T=13$ and $25/43$ ($58.1\%$) for Mistral-7B at $T=7$,

\label{app:repeated}

preceding tokens replace newly generated ones. Mean token log-probability

normalized by the length of the hidden-state vector, concentrates in
layers $12$ to $21$. Blocking the $32$ highest-ranked

\subsection{Source-cache repair and attention-path experiments}
\label{app:mechanism}

The focused Qwen3-8B/MedCalc experiments fix $\mathcal Q_0$, comprising
$124$ historical IDs from $14$ calculators, before inference. Four NVIDIA
RTX 4090 graphics processors each receive every fourth ID, using the
$1{,}536$-token protocol in Appendix~\ref{app:detail}.
Let $e_i^X$ be binary correctness for item $i$ in condition $X$, with
$0$ denoting no skill. Selection uses only fresh baselines:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{rep}}
=\{i\in\mathcal Q_0:e_i^D=1,\ e_i^R=e_i^0=0\}.
\label{eq:repair-set}
\end{equation}
Of $116$ donor-correct, receiver-incorrect items, $114$ also fail without
a skill. On these same $114$ items, every condition uses
$a_X(L)=|\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{rep}}|^{-1}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{rep}}}e_i^X(L)$.
All $372$ baseline generations agree
token-for-token between the two suites. The complete repair grid contains
$2{,}356$ generations, the path grid $1{,}488$, and worker identity checks
$100$. All $48$ own-state writebacks are token-exact.

Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism} and Table~\ref{tab:mechanism-contrasts} use this
rule for eight comparisons with separate candidates. Repair and path tests
share item IDs and baseline tokens within each row. Repair is measured
at $L8$, $L12$, $L16$ and $L24$, and path cuts at $L8$, $L16$ and $L24$.
Writes, masks and contrasts follow
Eqs.~\eqref{eq:cache}, \eqref{eq:reading-cut} and \eqref{eq:repair-effects}.

\paragraph{Qwen3-8B/MedCalc truncation sensitivity.}
We retain all intervention outcomes, including outputs stopped at the
generation limit, which we call truncated outputs. For the
prespecified difference between $SC$ and $S$ at layer $16$, the gain is $38.6$ percentage
points.
The corresponding accuracy interaction $\Gamma$ is $31.6$ points. $SC-(SC+\mathrm{cut})$ is $35.1$ points.
On the $96$ items with all three baselines untruncated, the $SC$ gain over $S$ is
$38.5$ points.
At layer $16$, $S$, $SC$ and $SC+\mathrm{cut}$ truncate $4$, $4$ and $3$ of $114$ outputs.
Scoring truncated $S$ answers as correct and truncated $SC$ answers as
incorrect still leaves a
$35.1$-point repair advantage. At layer $24$, $SC$ and $SC+\mathrm{cut}$ truncate $3$ and $28$
outputs and show no additional loss in measured accuracy.

At layer $24$, reader and source-self cuts retain $29/114$ and $110/114$
correct answers. Their loss difference is $71.1$ points.
Reader cuts truncate $21$ outputs. Counting all as correct still leaves
retention at $50/114$, below source-self retention $110/114$ (no truncation).
Both contrasts survive this worst-case reassignment. Experiment records retain counts for each condition, file checksums
and these sensitivity calculations.

\paragraph{Redundant combined cut.}
With causal attention and otherwise positionwise operations, earlier
tokens cannot read the skill. Persistent reading cuts also prevent its
changed states from reaching later tokens. Adding a within-skill cut
therefore leaves outputs unchanged by induction over layers and generated
tokens. We omit this redundant condition. The argument does not apply
when later reading is allowed.

\subsection{Complete-source and receiving-history controls}
\label{app:state-completeness}

\paragraph{Population and protocol.}
The additional Qwen3-8B/MedCalc study uses a frozen $124$-question pool
from $14$ calculator skills, selected using historical outcomes before
these interventions. No item is removed based on the new repair outcome.
The correct-skill donor answers $121/124$ correctly; the no-skill baseline
answers $4/124$. Wrong uses the original unrelated skill; Neutral uses a
predeclared unrelated natural-language document, not a guarantee of zero
influence. Source positions and prompt lengths are aligned. The protocol
uses BF16, eager attention, split prefill, greedy decoding and a $1536$
new-token limit. All $49$ conditions per item share this protocol.
Fresh screening for a correct donor and incorrect Wrong and no-skill
baselines retains $114$ questions, reproducing the earlier $L16$
$S/C/SC$ accuracies of $3.5/7.0/42.1\%$. Table~\ref{tab:state-completeness}
instead reports all $124$ items, including donor and receiver errors.

\paragraph{Source coverage and receiving history.}
Before continuation, $SC$ source K/V matches the donor elementwise at all
$36$ layers for both receivers and $L\in\{8,16,24\}$. A further explicit
all-layer source write leaves all $744$ paired generated token sequences
unchanged. Other prefix K/V need not match the donor and can vary with
intervention depth. Copying only those other positions gives $3/124$
and $10/124$ correct answers (Wrong/Neutral); copying the complete prefix
cache gives $121/124$ in both contexts and reproduces all donor tokens
($248/248$ pairs). This is a positive control using same-question donor
computation. Replacing all source KV and replaying the prompt after the
skill gives $120/124$ in both contexts. Only $48/124$ outputs per context
are token-identical to the donor, so replay is not an exact numerical
identity under BF16 and different prefill computation shapes.

\paragraph{Paired uncertainty and truncation.}
The $SC@8-SC@24$ accuracy difference is $66.1$ percentage points in Wrong
and $64.5$ in Neutral. Resampling whole skill groups with replacement
$10{,}000$ times gives exploratory $95\%$ percentile intervals of
$[49.3,78.5]$ and $[40.5,82.8]$ points. The signs are positive/tied/negative
in $12/2/0$ and $11/2/1$ of the $14$ groups, respectively.
No $SC@8$ output reaches the token cap; $SC@24$ has three capped outputs
in Wrong and none in Neutral. Assigning capped outcomes adversarially
against the difference still leaves gaps of $63.7$ and $64.5$ points.
These intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The small
number of groups and single model/task limit extrapolation.

\paragraph{Cache content and layer windows.}
Holding all-layer source coverage fixed, correct-skill KV yields
$29.8/25.0\%$ accuracy in Wrong/Neutral, versus $4.8/6.5\%$ for
unrelated-skill KV and $1.6/4.0\%$ for a second predeclared neutral
text's KV. The Wrong-to-Wrong source write is also a token-exact identity
control. Four equally sized eight-layer source writes, at layers
$0$--$7$, $8$--$15$, $16$--$23$ and $24$--$31$, yield
$3.2/3.2/1.6/4.0\%$ in Wrong and $0.8/4.0/4.8/5.6\%$ in Neutral.
These windows individually recover little; comparison with all $36$
layers does not identify the minimum required coverage because the write
budgets differ. Late $SC$ need not improve on $C_{\mathrm{all}}$:
at $L24$ in Wrong, accuracy is $25.8\%$ versus $29.8\%$.

\paragraph{Audit and scope.}
All $6076$ formal records and $14$ implementation-check records passed
full key-set, identity, source-write and file-hash checks. An independent
process regraded answers, with identical labels in forward and reverse
order. Cache-coverage claims use saved runtime elementwise checks, not
an offline re-execution of the model. The study does not repeat the full
transfer/knockout depth sweep, identify a unique semantic variable in
other-position caches, or validate the margin sufficient condition.

We evaluate $24$ matched conditions in each of the eight model/task cells
(Table~\ref{tab:state-completeness}). Qwen3-8B/MedCalc reuses its frozen
$124$-question/$14$-skill pool and broader $49$-condition experiment.
For the other seven cells, candidate IDs are fixed from pre-existing
historical baseline pools, using the first $124$ in their original order
when necessary. Input-length preflight excludes only one DeepSeek/MedCalc
question because prompt plus $1536$ output tokens exceed the model's
context limit. This leaves $456$ new model--question pairs. No item is
removed based on a new repair result, and the table retains fresh donor
and receiver baseline errors. These are selected populations, not full
benchmark estimates or $580$ independent unique questions across models.

Wrong uses the original unrelated skill; Neutral uses the same predeclared
unrelated natural-language document in every cell, truncated or repeated
to align source positions and prompt lengths. It is not guaranteed to
have zero influence. All within-cell conditions use BF16, eager attention,
split prefill, greedy decoding and a $1536$ new-token limit. The seven new
cells use RTX 4090 GPUs and the same container image; the Qwen3-8B/MedCalc
results are reused from its earlier run. TheoremQA resets the official
parser globals before every answer. Layer numbers index each model's
blocks, with $36$ layers for Qwen, $32$ for Mistral and Llama, and $30$ for DeepSeek. The fixed integer layers are not equal fractions of
model depth.
Fresh screening of the original Qwen3-8B/MedCalc pool retains $114$ items
and reproduces $L16$ $S/C/SC$ at $3.5/7.0/42.1\%$; the complete-source
tables instead retain all $124$ candidates. The other cells likewise use
their own fixed pools, so their denominators differ from the older repair
and path-cut screen in Table~\ref{tab:mechanism-contrasts}.

The $24$ conditions comprise four baselines (donor, Wrong, Neutral,

copying, other-position KV copying, complete-prefix KV copying, and
all-layer source copying followed by replay of the later prompt.

$SC$. Runtime elementwise checks find zero source discrepancies at all
layers in every measured $SC$ condition. The explicit rewrite preserves
all $3{,}480$ generated sequences across the eight cells. These identities
concern KV at skill positions, not all residual states or all prefix KV.

correct versus the donor's $61/63$; this one-item improvement does not
make replay equivalent to the donor. Different BF16 prefill computation
shapes can change individual token predictions.

and the benchmark scorers evaluate those answers. On the full MedCalc benchmark, Qwen3-8B

and $31.5\%$ with an unrelated skill.

in six of eight cells. The direction is mixed for Llama/TheoremQA

Qwen/TheoremQA's Neutral interval touches zero
(Appendix~\ref{app:state-completeness}). Thus the large Qwen3-8B/MedCalc
depth gap is not a uniform cross-model rule.

Copying the complete prefix KV instead reproduces donor tokens in all

the later prompt reaches within $4.2$ accuracy points of the donor in
every cell, although it is not a token-level identity. Together, these
controls identify receiving state outside the skill positions as a factor

controls remain a Qwen3-8B/MedCalc case study

\section{Conclusion}

Using a contextual skill and reusing its internal states are distinct
capabilities. Across four models and two benchmarks, state transfer
weakens before the original execution's dependence on skill attention,

information becomes harder to reuse while the skill remains useful.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Potential applications.}
Our findings suggest a way to evaluate the reuse of contextual skills.
Consider a Web agent that repeatedly follows the same instructions across
requests. A reusable internal representation would need to preserve task
performance in the receiving execution. Our results motivate evaluating
this transfer separately from the original execution's dependence on the
skill. If a reuse method also removes access to the original instructions,
that additional change needs its own evaluation. The observed cache gains
motivate reuse methods that carry both hidden states and attention caches
across requests. Deployment studies can evaluate their latency, memory
use and task performance in interactive Web settings.

\paragraph{Future work.}
A next step is to investigate which questions benefit from cache
replacement. The mathematical analysis connects remaining cache
differences to output stability under explicit assumptions. Measuring
these differences, their influence on token predictions and the donor's
prediction margins could test whether this framework helps distinguish
successful from unsuccessful repairs. The complete-source controls further motivate testing which parts of
the receiving history must be recomputed, and whether the required budget
can be predicted on held-out skills. Extending these controls beyond
Qwen3-8B/MedCalc would test their cross-model and cross-task scope. Separating attention cuts during prompt
processing from those during answer generation would clarify when continued
skill access matters. Finally,
multi-step Web workflows would assess how far the observed separation
extends beyond the question-answering settings studied here.
